Grecians
GREE-shunz
n. (Greek-speaking, Hellenized Jews, distinguished in Acts from the native Hebrew-speaking believers)
Greek Hellenistes (G1675), from Hellen, a Greek; rendered Grecians in the KJV to distinguish Greek-speaking Jews from ethnic Greeks (rendered "Greeks").

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Grecians of Acts are not ethnic Greeks but Greek-speaking, diaspora-formed Jews, and their first appearance exposes the earliest recorded internal tension in the New Testament church: “there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration” (Acts 6:1), the very occasion that produced the appointment of the first deacons (Acts 6:2–6). The distinction is cultural and linguistic, not doctrinal — both groups were Jewish believers in Jesus — yet it was real enough to require careful pastoral wisdom to resolve without division. The same word appears when Saul, newly converted, “spake boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus, and disputed against the Grecians: but they went about to slay him” (Acts 9:29), showing that unbelieving Hellenistic Jews could be as hostile to the gospel as any other quarter. The word turns in a wholly positive direction at Antioch, where believers scattered by persecution “spake unto the Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus” (Acts 11:20), the first recorded systematic preaching of Christ to a Hellenized, partly Gentile-adjacent audience, and the seed of the church that would send out Paul and Barnabas. Centuries earlier, Joel had already used the same underlying Hebrew concept of the Greeks (“the children of Judah and the children of Jerusalem have ye sold unto the Grecians,” Joel 3:6) as a byword for a distant, foreign slave market — the very people who, by Acts, had become some of the earliest hearers of the gospel that would one day be preached “to the Jew first, and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Grecian as a native of Greece, or one skilled in the Greek language; the New Testament word names Hellenized, Greek-speaking Jews, first appearing in the church's earliest internal conflict over neglected widows.

expand to see more

GRECIAN, n. A native of Greece; in Scripture, a Greek-speaking, Hellenized Jew of the dispersion, distinguished from native Hebrew-speaking Jews.

HEBREW, n. A descendant of Abraham; in Acts 6, specifically a native Aramaic or Hebrew-speaking Jew, as distinguished from a Grecian.

DEACON, n. A church officer whose office, first instituted in Acts 6, involves the care of the church's temporal and charitable needs.

DISPERSION, n. The scattering of the Jewish people among the Gentile nations; the setting that produced Greek-speaking Jewish communities.

MURMURING, n. Complaint uttered in a low, discontented tone; the sin Israel repeatedly committed in the wilderness, and a danger even within the early church.

Key Scripture

Acts 6:1 — "And in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplied, there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration."

Acts 9:29 — "And he spake boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus, and disputed against the Grecians: but they went about to slay him."

Acts 11:20 — "And some of them were men of Cyprus and Cyrene, which, when they were come to Antioch, spake unto the Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus."

Joel 3:6 — "The children also of Judah and the children of Jerusalem have ye sold unto the Grecians, that ye might remove them far from their border."

Modern Corruption

A narrative that records the earliest church's own internal ethnic-linguistic friction, rather than hiding it, is the mark of honest history, not a triumphalist later legend of the church's founding.

expand to see more

Modern intersectional readings eager to recast Acts 6 as a template for perpetual identity-based grievance politics within the church miss the text's actual resolution: the apostles did not form a permanent Grecian caucus or institutionalize the grievance, they appointed godly, Spirit-filled men (several bearing Greek names themselves, Acts 6:5) to serve both groups, and the murmuring ceased as the word of God increased (Acts 6:7). The biblical pattern is concrete, servant-hearted remedy under recognized church office, not the perpetuation of grievance as identity.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gospel does not erase cultural and linguistic distinctions among believers, but it does demand that no such distinction be allowed to produce practical injustice in the care of Christ's own people — the same gospel that produced murmuring Grecians in Acts 6 produced, within the same chapter, deacons appointed to serve them, and by Acts 11, Grecians themselves hearing and receiving the good news of the very Lord their fellow believers had once neglected them under.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Hellenistes (G1675), a Hellenist, Greek-speaking Jew, from Hellen (G1672), a Greek; gogguzo (G1111), to murmur; diakonia (G1248), ministry, service.

expand to see more

Greek Hellenistes (G1675) — a Hellenist; a Greek-speaking, culturally Hellenized Jew.

Greek Hellen (G1672) — a Greek; the root behind Hellenistes and behind the English Grecian.

Greek gogguzo (G1111) — to murmur; the sin named at the root of Acts 6:1, echoing Israel's wilderness murmuring.

Greek diakonia (G1248) — ministry, service; the daily distribution the Grecian widows were being denied.

Greek euangelizo (G2097) — to preach good news; the verb of Acts 11:20's turning point.

Usage

"“A murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews” — the church's earliest recorded internal conflict."

"“He... disputed against the Grecians: but they went about to slay him” — Saul's early, dangerous ministry."

"“Spake unto the Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus” — the gospel's advance at Antioch."
